newsitem.title: USA: Perdue Farms chief sees 8-10 percent sales growth.
newsitem.headline: Perdue Farms chief sees 8-10 percent sales growth.

text.p: Jim Perdue, chairman of Perdue Farms Inc, the nation's second largest poultry producer, predicted company sales would grow eight to ten percent a year over the next couple of years.

"I think not withstanding the kind of strange environment we're in right now, coming out of the grain situation and with meat supplies plentiful, we're probably projecting an eight to 10 percent growth a year in sales," he said in an interview.
The family-owned company, headquartered in Salisbury, Md., had sales of $2.1 billion in 1996, after growing the company by some 13 percent a year since 1991.

Perdue said that pace would be tough to maintain because overall growth in the U.S. poultry industry had slackened. Looking ahead, company strategy was to produce more value-added products versus more meat, and to build exports.
"The trend is pretty clear and that is convenience. People want to spend very little time, 20 minutes or so, cooking dinner," Perdue said.

New products include the "Boastin' Roaster", boneless roasting chicken meat wrapped in tin foil for easy cooking, seasoned whole chickens, meal kits with pasta and vegetables, cooked chicken with barbecue sauce and boxed kids' meals with a toy and a cookie alongside chicken nuggets.
Exports have become the fastest growing segment of Perdue's business, climbing to 10 percent of sales in 1996 compared with less than three percent five years ago.

Among its exports, Perdue Farms sells hot dogs and chicken quarters to Russia, chicken feet to China and cooked chicken legs to Japan. Next month, it expects to complete a 15-million-lb capacity freezer at the Norfolk, Va. port for exports.
Perdue said the company's 1995 purchase of rival producer Showell Farms helped boost exports.
The Showell, Md.-based company operated five plants and exports made up some 15 percent to 20 percent of its business.

"They had a better export business, much better than we did. And we continue to service those customers and grow the business with those customers with our cooking and value added capability which they didn't have," he said. "It was a good match. That really kind of helped boost our export business."
The recent dramatic decline in Russia poultry imports will likely keep 1997 exports around last year's pace, said Perdue. But he noted Russia imports were starting to pick up.

Perdue said he saw "tremendous markets" in South Korea and India as tariffs come down as part of the world trade agreement. He also listed South Africa, Eastern Europe and the Middle East as potential markets.
"The Middle East is an area that has been dominated by Europe more so than the United States so there's a lot of interest in the United States to send more product to the Middle East," he said.
Domestically, Perdue said the company did not have a plan to expand its retail business westward beyond Chicago.

Asked if the family-owned business might sell shares to the public, he said: "As long as we can fund our growth through borrowing and earnings which we've been able to do, I don't see any advantage to going public."
